analysis.one_liner: Strips insurance companies' federal antitrust immunity so they can be sued and prosecuted for price-fixing.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Democrat and cosponsored by two Democrats and two Republicans including the Senate Majority Leader, got a committee hearing in March 2007 but was never reported out or voted on before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, the McCarran-Ferguson Act has exempted the business of insurance from federal antitrust laws, letting insurers collectively set rates and share pricing data without facing price-fixing charges. This bill would amend that law so the Federal Trade Commission Act applies to insurance, giving the FTC and the Justice Department authority to police collusion among insurance companies. It was introduced by Sen. Patrick Leahy with two Republicans and two Democrats cosponsoring, held a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, and then sat without further action until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people and businesses who buy insurance. Insurers are exempt from the antitrust laws that apply to nearly every other industry, which lets them jointly set rates and exchange pricing data without legal consequence. Ending the exemption would let the FTC and Justice Department police price-fixing, bid-rigging, and market division among insurers, potentially lowering premiums and improving terms for policyholders.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so federal antitrust law (the FTC Act) reaches the business of insurance, removing the industry's blanket immunity from collusion laws.
Strikes section 3 of McCarran-Ferguson (15 U.S.C. 1013), the provision that shields insurers' joint rate-setting and data-sharing agreements from antitrust review.
Authorizes the Justice Department and FTC to issue joint statements of their antitrust enforcement policies on joint activities in insurance, giving insurers clear notice of what is illegal.

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which would lose their blanket immunity from federal antitrust enforcement and could be sued or prosecuted for colluding on rates, limiting competition, or dividing markets.

drawbacks.text: The bill keeps a large carve-out: the FTC Act would apply to insurance only 'to the extent that such business is not regulated by state law,' so insurers and their lawyers could argue that virtually any state regulation shields their conduct from federal antitrust scrutiny, blunting the bill's practical reach.

Critics of ending the McCarran-Ferguson exemption have long argued that insurers' joint sharing of loss and pricing data helps small insurers compete against big carriers and can keep premiums down; the bill strikes that exemption (15 U.S.C. 1013), which could deter useful joint activity along with collusion.

The bill would have had limited effect on health insurance in the near term, since the data-sharing immunity it strikes generally did not cover health insurance, and the FTC Act provisions it extends apply only where state regulation is absent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — giving antitrust enforcers power to police insurers' pricing and market-sharing agreements — is real and directly aimed at a cost households pay, but the bill as written leaves a state-regulation carve-out, so insurers could argue that any state oversight shields them from FTC action. The strongest good-faith objection is that blanket antitrust application could deter the joint actuarial data-sharing that helps small insurers price accurately in markets dominated by a few big carriers. On balance a modest, genuine consumer-protection measure that appears to have been set aside despite bipartisan sponsorship.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held a hearing on it in March 2007, but the committee never reported it to the full Senate and no vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. Leahy on February 15, 2007, and read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The Judiciary Committee held a hearing on March 7, 2007 — the only action beyond referral in the bill's two-year life.
No markup was scheduled and the bill was never reported to the floor; it died at the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.
The bill was bipartisan from the start: Leahy introduced it with Republican Sens. Specter and Lott and Democrats Reid and Landrieu.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The insurance industry is better off: its blanket antitrust immunity under McCarran-Ferguson survived, and no insurance company faced the added federal antitrust exposure the bill would have created.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: Senate bill sponsor; Chairman, Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the committee that held a hearing on it, but did not report it to the floor.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill; as Majority Leader he never brought it to a floor vote.

for.name: Sens. Arlen Specter and Trent Lott
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Patrick Leahy)
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing on March 7, 2007 but never scheduled a markup or reported the bill to the Senate floor.

against.name: Insurance industry and allied trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed repeal of the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, arguing that joint rate data-sharing benefits consumers and that the industry is already regulated by the states.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from introduction: two Republicans (Specter, Lott) and two Democrats (Reid, Landrieu) joined sponsor Leahy, and the bill's death involved no roll-call votes at any stage.

industries.note: The bill would strip the industry's decades-old blanket antitrust exemption under McCarran-Ferguson, exposing rate-setting agreements, data-sharing cartels, and market allocation to DOJ and FTC enforcement. Its interest runs against ordinary policyholders because the immunity it kept made it easier to coordinate prices on products consumers are legally required to buy.
